text: Label leakage and ambiguity: SEND is defined by the outcome (scored or out at home), so SEND is not the coach's decision. The feasibility sample shows "advanced later" at 26 (2025) and 21 (2026) of 85/90 opportunities, so a large share of the SEND class is the ambiguous class. CITE: feasibility-sample

Counting "advanced later" runners as SEND in the primary analysis probably contaminates the label. The feed says these cases leave the send decision ambiguous, and a runner who stopped at third and scored on a wild pitch or a subsequent hit is a hold. CITE: feasibility-sample

Strict sends are 14 safe and 0 out in 2025, and 12 safe and 0 out in 2026. Out-at-home is 0 in both seasons, so the early-stop rule (fewer than 30 SEND runners thrown out at home in 2025) will almost surely trigger on the sample rates. Full-season data is only about 24 times larger, so the model may well not be fit. The design should state the expected outcome of its own stop rule. CITE: feasibility-sample

If "advanced later" is counted as SEND, the early stop is still driven by outs at home, which stay 0 in the sample. P(safe | SEND) then has almost no variation to model, and the Brier-versus-constant test has little power. Success on that test would more likely reflect noise or the label mixing than skill. CITE: feasibility-sample

The stop rule is gameable and ambiguous. It is unclear whether the 30-out threshold is evaluated under the primary or the sensitivity label. It is also unclear whether it counts league-wide or only fully identified runners (fielder ID is 91.8% and 86.7%). A choice among these definitions after seeing counts would change the branch taken. CITE: feasibility-sample

Base-at-contact is inferred from originBase of the first segment. The feed does not establish the base at the exact batted-ball moment, so the design's claim of validation in R3-S2 is unverified. CITE: feasibility-sample

qualifying-opportunity counts. This report gets 85 and 90 under the first-segment rule, the controller's recount gets 88 and 95, and the diagnostic any-segment rule gets 88 and 95. The scored and held counts also disagree (2025 scored 40 vs 35; 2026 held 56 vs 58). The population definition is unsettled, and the design never says which one binds. CITE: feasibility-sample

The first-segment rule excludes runners whose 1B>2B segment preceded a later threshold segment, but this is not shown to be correct rather than merely documented. Excluded runners may be systematically the ones on multi-base plays, which would bias the sample toward certain hit types. CITE: feasibility-sample

Selection bias: holds are defined by where the runner ended, but the sample's sends are almost all safe, so a model of P(safe | SEND) learns only the covariate region where coaches already send. Holds are mostly the 44 and 56 runners, and extrapolating to them is outside the support. The 2.5th to 97.5th percentile marginal range check is inadequate, because per-covariate ranges can contain a joint region with no sends (for example slow runner, short throw, shallow location). Marginal overlap does not establish joint overlap. CITE: feasibility-sample

Replace the marginal percentile check with a joint overlap check, for example a propensity or density-ratio model for send versus hold, with holds trimmed where the estimated send probability is very low. Report the share of holds retained.

With about zero outs at home among sends, the logistic model cannot separate "safe" from "all safe". If safe approaches 100%, then p is near 1 for most holds and nearly every hold is flagged, so runs-left is driven by the break-even formula rather than the covariates. The result would be a false positive. CITE: feasibility-sample

The break-even formula is likely incomplete. With RE[run scored state] + 1 as the send-safe value, the formula omits the batter's advance to second on a throw, the trail runner's outcome, and an error on the throw. It also omits the ordering of outs: the hold state and the out-at-home state depend on the number of outs, so RE must be state-specific. The text says trailing runners are ignored, so the run-value accounting is acknowledged as partial, and the direction of that bias is unstated.

Break-even algebra check needed. Sending gains p(RE_s + 1) + (1 - p)RE_o and holding gives RE_h, so p* = (RE_h - RE_o) / (RE_s + 1 - RE_o). This matches the design's formula for a single runner. It treats the safe outcome as a state where the runner scored, but the "safe" state also includes the batter's base, which is not modeled, and the formula omits that.
RE fit on 2025 only is noisy for sparse states (for example runner on third with two outs after a trailing runner). The design gives no minimum cell count, smoothing, or handling of empty cells.

Success criteria permit a false positive. Runs-left is a sum over flagged holds, with flagging at p ≥ p* + 0.05 using the same noisy p. This is a winner's-curse selection: choosing holds where p is high selects model-error upside. The bootstrap interval excluding zero would then follow mechanically. Holdout calibration on sends does not validate predictions on holds.

Power is poor for the holdout. The Brier and calibration tests use 2026 sends, which total 12 safe and 0 out in the sample. With no or very few outs, the calibration slope is unstable or undefined, and a slope range of 0.7 to 1.3 is not testable at this size. The design reports no power calculation. CITE: feasibility-sample

Expected number of SEND runners and outs at home across the two full seasons beyond a naive scaling of the sample. The league-wide opportunity interval of about 3257–5005 (2025) and 3157–5591 (2026) is wide and assumes normal sampling without schedule-date adjustment. CITE: feasibility-sample

The feed does not establish the coach's sign, the runner's jump, or the counterfactual for held runners. Some holds are forced by a cutoff, the batter's own position, or the ball in front of the runner, so "missed send" may be mislabeled. A third-base coach cannot act on a result that cannot distinguish a coach's decision from a runner's own stop. CITE: feasibility-sample

Season-level sprint speed and arm strength use post-decision information, and the design says this is "identical for sends and holds". That is unproven, because the matching rate differs: arm strength matches 50/54 and 47/52, and infield-fielded balls are missing. Missingness correlates with hit location and with the hold rate. A missing flag does not remove this confound. CITE: feasibility-sample

Decision-time usability: the coach does not know the exact hit location, the fielder's arm value, or a model score in real time. Without a pre-play lookup table (runner by fielder zone), a third-base coach cannot use the result. The Cubs-only count is descriptive and has too few cases for guidance.

Make the primary label a strict one: SEND only when the runner scores or is out at home on the same batted-ball segment, with "advanced later" excluded and reported as a third category, and with a pre-registered rule for counting outs at home so the stop condition is unambiguous.

Pre-register a single population definition, resolve the 85/88 and 90/95 discrepancy by reconciling against a sample of play-level cases before the full data pull, and fix the stop rule's inputs as league-wide strict sends in 2025.

Replace "runs-left interval excludes zero" with a sensitivity band across break-even assumptions (trailing runner, batter advance, error rate) and an interval from a conservative model, and require a positive result under the strict label and the joint-overlap trim together.

Whether any out at home occurs at all in the full seasons, and thus whether this design can ever fit the model it describes. The sample shows 0 outs at home among strict sends. CITE: feasibility-sample

Zero SEND runners were thrown out at home in the feasibility sample (sent out = 0 in both 2025 and 2026; out at home = 0.0%). The early-stop rule of 30 outs at home in 2025 is likely to fail or be borderline, and the design does not state what the fallback result is worth to a coach. CITE: feasibility-sample
85 * 0.0 = 0 observed sent-out in the 2025 sample; sent safe 14 of 85 opportunities

Extrapolating to a full season is speculative. The sample shows no outs at home, and the full-season count of 30 depends on a rate the sample cannot bound. It may also never be reached, which makes DESCRIPTIVE ONLY the likely outcome rather than a rare fallback. CITE: feasibility-sample

The SEND label mixes two things. "Sent safe" (14 in 2025) is a clear send. The "advanced later" class (26 in 2025) is larger and is folded into SEND by default. Those runners stopped at third and scored on a later event (wild pitch, error, next batter), so they are not sends. The primary analysis would then be dominated by holds mislabeled as sends and would inflate P(safe). The sensitivity analysis should be primary, or the class should be excluded. CITE: feasibility-sample

The count of "scored (any)" (40) and "ended at 3B, no score" (44) are overlapping views, not partitions. The label rules (SEND = ends in scoring; HOLD = ends at third and not out) are ambiguous for runners who appear in both. HOLD as defined can include runners who later scored, and the label order is not specified. CITE: feasibility-sample

Counts disagree with the controller's recount (2025: 85 vs 88 opportunities, 40 vs 35 scored; 2026: 90 vs 95 opportunities, 33 vs 35 scored). The first-segment rule is described as "validated in R3-S2", but the evidence shows the recount differs and its method is unverified. The qualifying-population definition is therefore not settled. CITE: feasibility-sample
qualifying_opportunities_and_scored_counts_between_report_and_controller_recount

Base at contact is inferred from originBase, not observed. Runners excluded under the first-segment rule include some with "1B>2B" contact bases, which suggests the inferred base can be wrong when the feed records several segments. The "single with runner on second, double with runner on first" population may include misclassified plays. CITE: feasibility-sample

Candidate opportunities are not confirmed as coach decisions. The feed does not record the coach's sign, the runner's jump, or the counterfactual for holds. Many holds may be forced (ball played to a fielder with no chance, or a runner stopped by a base-running decision before the coach's view). The study estimates "holds with high modeled P(safe)", not "coach errors". CITE: feasibility-sample

Fewer than two outs is part of the decision rule, but the feasibility table does not report the out distribution. Run-expectancy break-even differs strongly by outs. The outs filter and its sample counts are unverified. UNKNOWN is better than assumed. CITE: feasibility-sample
outs_distribution_of_qualifying_opportunities

The break-even formula is p* = (RE[hold] - RE[out]) / (RE[scored]+1 - RE[out]). The "+1" is the run itself. When the runner is thrown out at home, the batter may also advance (trail runner), which RE[out state] ignores, and the batter's base after the throw is a decision too. Omitting trailing runners biases p* in an unknown direction. The hold state should be the actual hold base-out state, including the batter's actual base, which the design does not say. The inning, score difference, and late-game leverage (win probability) are ignored, so run value may not match what a coach should maximize.

The runs-left sum treats RE tables from a single season (2025) as truth for 2026 holdout valuation and ignores RE sampling error in the bootstrap. The game bootstrap covers only game resampling, so the interval is too narrow. It also treats the p estimates as exact for every flagged hold.

Selecting holds by predicted P(safe) >= p* + 0.05 and then summing the gain is a winner's-curse setup. Noise in the model pushes holds above the threshold, so the sum is positive even for a useless model. A "95% interval excluding zero" is therefore a likely false-positive path, particularly because gain is only summed over flagged holds and never offset by unflagged ones or by sends that would have been wrong. Negative-expected-value sends are never counted. CITE: feasibility-sample

Selection bias is directional and severe. Sends in the sample are few (14 safe in 2025, 12 in 2026, no outs), so the model is learned from near-all-successes. Logistic regression on a near-constant label cannot rank risk, and a model fit with zero or very few failures will predict high P(safe) everywhere, flagging nearly every hold. Brier win over the constant baseline is not a power check for this. CITE: feasibility-sample

The overlap check uses per-covariate 2.5th to 97.5th percentile marginals. Marginal ranges can pass while the joint combination (slow runner, deep arm, shallow ball) is unsupported. It also does not weight by density; a hold in a region with 2 sends passes. Reporting only inside-range holds changes the estimand and is not stated as such. A joint check (for example, a classifier of send vs hold or a Mahalanobis or nearest-neighbor distance) would be stronger.

Replace the marginal overlap check with a send-vs-hold propensity model and report only holds with propensity within the support of sends. Require a minimum count of sends in the neighborhood, and report the share of holds dropped.

Leakage: season-level sprint speed and arm strength include the play outcomes themselves (a runner sent and safe adds to sprint speed estimates) and later-season information. The design calls this identical for sends and holds, but that is unverified; it is not identical when speed estimates are measured from competitive runs. Arm strength is missing for infielders (fielder ID 91.8% in 2025, 86.7% in 2026; arm match 92.6% and 90.4%). Missingness is tied to hit location, so it is not random. CITE: feasibility-sample

Fitting on 2025 and validating on 2026 is a clear split, but gaming paths remain. The "freeze hash" covers the model and thresholds, but not the label rules, exclusion rules, or the 0.05 margin. The label rules could be changed after seeing the 2025 full data, since the SEND/HOLD classifier was validated on the feasibility sample, which contains both seasons. The feasibility sample already includes 2026 outcomes, so 2026 is not untouched. CITE: feasibility-sample

Holdout validity is tested only on 2026 SEND runners, which are the 12 sampled safe sends scaled to a season. The calibration slope window 0.7 to 1.3 is wide and unstable with a small number of failures. Slope is not defined with zero failures. A pass reflects the model's ability to rank sends, not holds, and says nothing about holds' P(safe). CITE: feasibility-sample

Cubs results are descriptive only, with small counts (a fraction of league-wide opportunities of about 4100 to 4400), so the team-level number is mostly noise, and a coach could not act on it. The design does not give a sample-size minimum before reporting a Cubs number. CITE: feasibility-sample

League-wide opportunity estimates are rough (2025: 4131, interval 3257 to 5005; 2026: 4374, interval 3157 to 5591) because they come from 50 games per season and ignore schedule-date effects. Planning with these figures overstates precision. CITE: feasibility-sample

The result could be useless to a third-base coach. The coach acts on information before the throw (outfielder position, depth, wind, the runner's jump, who is up next). The design uses ball location, fielder arm, and season-level speed, but lacks fielder position, pre-pitch alignment, and throw outcome. A "missed send" is judged by hindsight information the coach did not have in real time (final fielder ID is known only after the play). It also reports averages rather than a rule or threshold the coach can use in-game. CITE: feasibility-sample

Add a pre-registered decision chart: P(safe) bands by hit location, hit type, outs, and runner speed tercile, with the break-even p* for each cell, so a coach gets a usable lookup instead of a season-level runs total.

Use a negative-control check. Apply the same flagging procedure to a placebo where the label is shuffled within game-season strata, or to sends only (cross-fitted), and require the real runs-left estimate to exceed the placebo distribution.

Make the 30-out-at-home early stop a count-based rule on the 2025 data with explicit fallback, and add a minimum failures-per-covariate rule (for example, events-per-variable) so the logistic model is not fit on near-zero failures. If unmet, penalize the model or reduce covariates.

Define label precedence explicitly. Order by final outcome: out at home, then scored in the same segment as the batted-ball play (SEND), then stopped at third (HOLD), with "advanced later" as its own excluded class in the primary analysis.
Put the first-segment base rule, exclusions, 0.05 margin, and the label precedence into the frozen hash before the full 2025 data is opened, and reconcile the controller recount before the full pull.

The early-stop rule (fewer than 30 SEND runners thrown out at home in 2025) is almost certainly triggered. CITE: feasibility-sample shows out-at-home = 0 in the 85 sampled 2025 opportunities and 0 in 2026, "sent out" = 0 in both seasons. The sample is about 3.5% of games (50 of roughly 2,433), so the full-season count would need to reach 30, which is not supported by the sample.
expected_2025_out_at_home_count_full_season (a zero count in the sample gives only a weak upper bound, and no estimate can be made from it).

If the early stop fires, the whole success-model, holdout, and runs-left chain is moot, and the study reduces to a descriptive report. The design should state this as the likely outcome in advance, not as a remote contingency. CITE: feasibility-sample

The 30-out threshold is a counts-based rule, not a power calculation. With a SEND-out rate near zero, a logistic model of P(safe | SEND) has almost no negative class. This makes calibration slope and Brier comparisons against a constant baseline uninformative even if the 30 threshold is just met. CITE: feasibility-sample

The SEND label is ambiguous and may inflate the safe class. "Advanced later" runners (26 in 2025, 21 in 2026) are folded into SEND as primary. The feed does not establish whether these runners were sent, and they stopped at third first. CITE: feasibility-sample. Because the sample "sent safe" is only 14 and 12 and "advanced later" is 26 and 21, the primary SEND class would be about two-thirds ambiguous. The primary analysis is therefore driven by the ambiguous label, and the sensitivity analysis would be the closer approximation to real sends.

Counting a runner who stopped at third and later scored (for example on a wild pitch, balk, or sacrifice fly) as a successful send biases P(safe | SEND) upward. It also labels holds as sends when the coach actually held, which contaminates the HOLD class and understates holds. CITE: feasibility-sample

The HOLD label "ends at third and is not out" cannot separate a coach hold from a runner who was sent and stopped, or from a play where the batter was thrown out and the runner was forced to stay. The feed does not record the coach's sign or the jump. CITE: feasibility-sample

opportunity_and_movement_counts (this report: 85 and 90 opportunities, 40 and 33 scored (any), 44 and 56 ended at 3B. Controller recount: 88 and 95, 35 and 35, 47 and 58). The design cites "rule validated in R3-S2", but the evidence shows the recount did not reproduce the movement views. CITE: feasibility-sample

The first-segment base-at-contact rule is inferred from originBase and excludes runners such as those listed as 1B>2B in a single contact. The design's claim of validation is unsupported, since the controller's totals match the any-segment rule. The qualifying set depends on an unresolved definition, and the analyst can choose either definition after seeing results. CITE: feasibility-sample

The "scored (any)" and "ended at 3B" counts are not partitions. Using them as labels without whole-play disambiguation will double count runners. The design should define a single mutually exclusive label hierarchy before any data is retrieved. CITE: feasibility-sample

Fielder ID is 91.8% and 86.7%, and arm-strength leaderboard matches are 92.6% and 90.4%. The design says arm values are "missing for infielders", but the missingness here also arises from ID and join failures and is probably not random relative to hit location. Dropping or flagging these rows could shift the sample toward outfield-hit plays, where the arm covariate is defined. CITE: feasibility-sample

Season-level speed and arm values are computed using the very plays being evaluated, so they are not purely pre-decision information. The design calls this "identical for sends and holds", but that is unproven. The leaked values could favor a send or a hold differently, because a runner who was sent and safe adds to his own leaderboard record. This invalidates the claim of equal leakage. CITE: feasibility-sample

The holdout split is a single season-to-season shift. The 2025 run-expectancy table and model are applied to 2026, which has a different hold rate (62.2% vs 51.8%) and a different advanced-later rate (23.3% vs 30.6%). This could reflect a rule, ball, or coaching change, or a labeling difference, and the design has no stability check before the holdout is run. CITE: feasibility-sample

The break-even formula treats the out-at-home state as RE with an added out, but does not say whether the batter's advance to second on the throw is included. It ignores trailing runners, the possibility of the batter taking an extra base on the throw, and runners who are held on a send that was drawn off. The formula also omits the score-difference and inning effects (late-inning leverage). These omissions bias the break-even in a direction that is not stated. The RE table for the "run scored state" must also specify the new base-out state with the count of outs held fixed. CITE: feasibility-sample

The runs-left sum uses model p, which is extrapolated from sends. Flagging holds where p is at least p* + 0.05 selects on estimation noise, so the maximum of noisy estimates has a positive bias (winner's curse). The interval from a game bootstrap that doesn't refit the model would understate the uncertainty. This could give a false positive. The 0.05 margin is arbitrary and was not fixed from any data or power rationale.

The positive criterion requires only that the runs-left interval exclude zero. The sum of terms, each defined as at least a margin above break-even by the model's own estimate, is positive by construction. An interval that excludes zero is therefore almost guaranteed given enough flagged holds, even if the model is wrong. The test needs a falsifiable benchmark, such as a placebo or a model calibrated on outcomes that is not selected on the flag.

The overlap check uses per-covariate marginal percentile ranges. This does not detect joint extrapolation, such as a slow runner with a deep hit to a weak arm, and holds with no sends nearby remain. The check should be joint (for example, nearest-neighbor distance or a propensity or density model), and the counts excluded should be reported. CITE: feasibility-sample

The selection of sends is on information the coach uses and the model lacks (jump, outfielder position, throw angle). Even inside the overlap range, the P(safe | SEND) estimate is conditional on the coach choosing to send. For the holds, the unobserved features are the reason they were held. The result can only be an upper bound, and the "missed send" labeling may be unfounded. CITE: feasibility-sample
counterfactual_outcome_for_held_runners (the feed does not establish it). CITE: feasibility-sample
coach_sign_and_runner_jump (not in feed). CITE: feasibility-sample

The sample shows 14 and 12 safe sends against 0 outs at home. With that, the observed out rate in sends is below p* for nearly any hold. A model fit to near-zero failures would predict P(safe) close to 1 for most covariates and flag most holds. This makes the runs-left figure a function of the coaches' selective sending, not evidence of missed sends. The result would be useless for a third-base coach if it simply says to send everyone. CITE: feasibility-sample

The result may be useless to a third-base coach in practice, since the model uses end-of-season speed and arm values, post-hoc hit coordinates, and a model not given the outfielder's position or the on-field state at decision time. A coach cannot use a P(safe) from these. It also yields no per-situation decision rule, only a league-wide aggregate. The Cubs-only counts are descriptive with small samples. CITE: feasibility-sample

Request budget: the estimated 4,866 requests for the full retrieval is far above the 150 allowance, and 107 were used in the sample. The design says about 2,433 per season, but the estimate for the full two-season schedule and leaderboards is 4,866. The retrieval plan is not shown to be feasible within any stated limit, and a partial fetch could introduce a non-random subset. CITE: feasibility-sample

The league-wide opportunity estimates (4131 and 4374, with intervals [3257, 5005] and [3157, 5591]) are scaled from 50 games and are not adjusted for date effects. They overlap widely, so no between-season claim is supported. Because of the labeling disagreement (85 vs 88), the scale could also shift. CITE: feasibility-sample

Freeze one mutually exclusive label hierarchy (coach-held, sent-safe, sent-out, ambiguous-advanced-later) and the base-at-contact definition before retrieval. Resolve the controller-versus-report discrepancy on the cached sample first, and make ambiguous runners a third class instead of folding them into SEND.

Replace the stop rule with a precomputed power rule. Require a minimum number of out-at-home events in the pooled 2025 and 2026 data, and state in advance that a likely outcome is DESCRIPTIVE ONLY. Report the observed out rate with an exact upper bound.

Make the positive criterion falsifiable by refitting the model inside each bootstrap, replacing the 0.05 margin with a pre-set value tested on the held-out data, and adding a negative control (for example, applying the flag rule to sends and checking if realized outcomes match predicted success).
Use a joint overlap measure and decision-time covariates (prior-season speed and arm values) so the model does not use the same-season information.
